title: The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation
research_question: What are the effects of expanding access to group-lending microcredit on household borrowing, business creation and performance, consumption patterns, labor supply, and broader social outcomes such as education, health, and women's empowerment? Do these effects persist or change as borrowers gain longer exposure to microcredit?
data_description: The study uses primary household survey data collected in 104 poor neighborhoods (bastis) of Hyderabad, India, in collaboration with the Centre for Micro Finance (CMF) at IFMR Chennai and the MFI Spandana. A baseline survey of about 2,800 households was conducted in 2005. A neighborhood census was done in 2007 to construct an endline sampling frame focused on likely borrowers (resident at least three years, containing a woman aged 18–55). A first endline surveyed approximately 6,850 households 15–18 months after microcredit introduction (Aug 2007–Apr 2008), and a second endline re-surveyed the same households in 2009–2010 with about 90% re-contact. Variables include household composition, borrowing from MFIs, banks, and informal sources; loan amounts; business ownership, assets, revenues, expenses, profits, and employees; labor supply; per capita consumption (durables, nondurables, food, temptation goods, festivals); education, health, and women's decision-making outcomes. Unit of observation: household.
institutional_context: The setting is Hyderabad, capital of Andhra Pradesh, India's fifth largest city, during a period of rapid economic growth (2005–2010) preceding the 2010 Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis. Spandana, then one of India's largest and fastest-growing for-profit MFIs, offered a canonical Grameen-style group-lending product: groups of 6–10 women jointly liable for 50-week loans starting at Rs. 10,000 (about $1,000 PPP) at a 24% APR, with eligibility restricted to women aged 18–59 who were long-term residents and largely homeowners. Spandana did not require business plans, training, or 'transformation' rituals, focusing purely on lending. The 104 study neighborhoods were marginal slums Spandana was indifferent about entering, lacked prior MFI presence, and contained poor but not destitute residents. Spandana progressively opened branches in 52 neighborhoods during 2006–2007, while other MFIs gradually entered both sets of neighborhoods over time.
